text: Everything so far in this chapter has been about making a training job run fast across many GPUs. This lesson is about making it survive — because on a run lasting days or weeks, something eventually breaks, and the question is how much progress that costs you.

A single GPU might go months between issues. A cluster of five hundred or a thousand GPUs, running continuously for weeks, doesn't get that luxury — with that many GPUs, NICs, and nodes, each carrying some nonzero failure rate, plus spot preemption, driver crashes, and NCCL errors on top, at least one failure during the run becomes likely, not exceptional. Without any fault-tolerance plan, a failure on day twelve of a three-week run means losing all twelve days and starting over.

Checkpointing exists to make that cost minutes, not days — but a real checkpoint has to capture more than the model weights. Optimizer state has to be saved too, or resumed training effectively restarts the optimizer and destabilizes. The step counter has to be saved so the learning-rate schedule picks up where it left off. RNG state and the data loader's position matter too, so resuming doesn't skip or re-feed training data unpredictably.

Checkpointing isn't free, though. Writing a large model's full state to durable storage takes real time and bandwidth, and if that write blocks training, you're burning GPU time on every single checkpoint. Checkpoint too rarely, and a failure costs more progress. Checkpoint too often, and the overhead itself slows the run down even when nothing fails. Asynchronous checkpointing is the common fix — write to fast local memory first, let training continue immediately, and flush to durable storage in the background.

This is the exact same trade-off this path already covered as RPO and RTO in resilience and disaster recovery, just applied to a training job instead of a production system. Checkpoint interval is your RPO — checkpoint every thirty minutes, and you can lose at most thirty minutes of progress to any single failure. The time to detect a failure, restart, and reload the last checkpoint is your RTO. A well-run training job picks that interval deliberately, based on what a failure actually costs — not by accident.
